problem: Existing VLN agents (e.g. HAMT) and SLAM systems are trained and evaluated in static environments, so they degrade when humans performing actions appear along the path, and they cannot recognize those actions. Simulators such as Matterport3D contain no human actions.
motivation: Visually impaired people cannot navigate dynamic spaces independently, and a survey by the author found that navigation and human action recognition are top difficulties. An assistive system needs to plan routes from language instructions while also being aware of surrounding people's actions.
key_idea: Add a ViT-based human action recognition branch to HAMT so navigation and action recognition share a cross-modal transformer backbone, and train it in Matterport3D augmented with generated 3D human actions (VAE + SMPL).
insight: Ablations (Table 2) show that adding an action recognition module to HAMT improves dynamic navigation, and ViT is best (SR seen 69.1 vs 67.3 for STGCN and 61.3 for the HAMT baseline). Cross-modal encoding between the navigation and action branches adds a further 3-4 points (Table 3: SR seen 69.1 to 73.2). Caveat: the evaluation is on the author's own simulator with self-generated humans and seems to be self-reported, so gains are not comparable with standard R2R numbers.
method: HAMT navigation backbone: history-aware multimodal transformer encoding instruction text, hierarchical panoramic history (ViT per image, then panorama-level, then temporal) and current view via a cross-modal encoder.

ViT action recognition branch: added into HAMT and sharing the ViT backbone, so the agent jointly reads action videos and performs navigation and action recognition. It reaches 76% action accuracy versus 59% for ST-GCN in their simulator.
Action Generator: a self-supervised VAE produces diverse action skeletons and SMPL renders 3D skinned bodies for 52 action types with over 20,000 poses.

Action-based simulator: Scene Discriminator picks the trajectories/viewpoints for placing humans and Scene Fusion blends them into Matterport3D, giving 1,050 viewpoints and over 10,000 images with humans.
RL training: the agent is trained with reinforcement learning for over 200,000 iterations in the action-based simulator.
New benchmark metrics: Completeness (percentage of complete action observations along the path) and Accuracy (correct action observations along the path).
Deployment: a cloud-client system with a mobile app and glasses camera, with the AAVLN model served through Flask.

numbers_note: Results are on the authors' custom action-based simulator, so the R2R rows are not comparable to standard R2R leaderboard numbers. Table 1 also lists bracketed static-environment baseline numbers for other methods (not reported as own). NE and other standard metrics are not reported.
results: In the authors' human-action simulator, AAVLN reaches SR/SPL 73.2/69.5 (seen) and 62.0/58.8 (unseen), against the strongest baseline HAMT (with mask) at 61.3/55.1 and 49.2/43.8. Ablations show ViT beats STGCN, InfoGCN and STRNN as the action module, and cross-modal encoding adds about 3-4 points.
limitations: Evaluation is only in the authors' own synthetic simulator with generated humans (no standard R2R, no real-world quantitative results), and baselines are apparently re-run or degraded, so the claims are hard to verify.
Insufficient methodological detail (RL formulation, rewards, how action video is fed in), and the text is inconsistent, e.g. the ablation percentages are mislabeled.
Humans are static posed 3D figures, so truly dynamic motion is not modeled, and there is no real-robot or user study data.
